hist.feature.name: Historical events
hist.feature.desc: A calendar of real events of the industry, 1971-2025: booms and crises, antitrust cases, export controls, price wars, patent disputes. The events find their participants in your game.
hist.param.mode.label: History mode (0 = adaptive, 1 = strict)
hist.param.mode.tooltip: 0 = adaptive: when the historical company is not in your game, the role goes to a fitting one. 1 = strict: an event happens only to those who were in the history, otherwise you get a "did not happen" news item.
hist.param.intensity.label: Effect intensity
hist.param.intensity.tooltip: The size of the effects of historical events, from 0.5 to 1.5. 1.0 is as designed in the calendar.
hist.param.macro.label: Category: macroeconomy
hist.param.macro.tooltip: Oil embargo, crises, trade wars: demand, credit and production cost.
hist.param.boom.label: Category: booms
hist.param.boom.tooltip: Releases of landmark platforms and products, growth of demand in segments.
hist.param.shock.label: Category: supply shocks
hist.param.shock.tooltip: Memory and chip shortages, higher production cost and output changes.
hist.param.disaster.label: Category: disasters and the pandemic
hist.param.disaster.tooltip: Earthquakes, tsunamis and the pandemic. Off by default.
hist.param.antitrust.label: Category: antitrust cases
hist.param.antitrust.tooltip: Cases against the market leader, fines, appeals and the surcharge on acquisition prices.
hist.param.export.label: Category: export controls
hist.param.export.tooltip: Limits on advanced chips and sanctions against single companies.
hist.param.priceWar.label: Category: price wars
hist.param.priceWar.tooltip: Aggressive price cuts by the leader and the answer of the competitors.
hist.param.patent.label: Category: patent disputes
hist.param.patent.tooltip: Disputes over licenses and design copying between companies.
hist.param.flaw.label: Category: processor flaws
hist.param.flaw.tooltip: Calculation errors and vulnerabilities found after release.
hist.param.race.label: Category: specification races
hist.param.race.tooltip: The race for frequency and cores: a rating bonus for the best processors.
hist.param.brand.label: Category: brand programs
hist.param.brand.tooltip: Marketing programs of the leader and joint marketing.
hist.param.oem.label: Category: OEM market
hist.param.oem.tooltip: Customers changing architecture and moving to their own processors.
hist.param.historyNotes.label: "How it really was" notes
hist.param.historyNotes.tooltip: Show a note about the real events and its sources in the letters about events.
hist.param.spoilers.label: Show future events
hist.param.spoilers.tooltip: Show events that have not happened yet in the industry chronicle.
hist.param.debug.label: Debug
hist.param.debug.tooltip: The chronicle page gets buttons to fire an event and to make the player a role. For checking only.

hist.2009.eufine.title: The European Commission fines {1}
hist.2009.eufine.fact: In 2009 the EC fined Intel EUR 1.06 bn over exclusivity rebates. A court annulled it in 2022; part was re-imposed in 2023 and reduced in 2024.
hist.decide.antitrust.fine.text: The regulator found {1} abusing dominance. Appeal: court ruling in about 5 years, monthly bank guarantee fee.{6}
hist.1998.ftc.title: The Federal Trade Commission opens a case against {1}
hist.1998.ftc.fact: In 1998 the US Federal Trade Commission opened an antitrust case against Intel; it ended in a settlement in 1999. The settlement required changes to some of its processor sales terms.
hist.decide.antitrust.consent.text: The antitrust regulator has opened a case against {1}. You can sign a settlement that limits the terms of contracts, or fight in court: the trial costs money, and a loss brings both the limits and a fine.{6}
hist.decide.antitrust.reimpose.title: A new fine for {1}
hist.decide.antitrust.reimpose.text: The earlier fine was annulled, but the regulator has imposed a new, smaller one. You can pay it at once or appeal again.{6}
hist.2009.settlement.title: A suit against {2} after the regulator's decision
hist.2009.settlement.fact: In 2009 AMD and Intel settled a long dispute: Intel paid AMD USD 1.25 bn. The dispute concerned rebates and other terms that restricted AMD's sales.
hist.decide.settlement.text: After the regulator's decision {1} can sue {2} for the damage of unfair competition. The trial takes about a year and costs legal fees; if it wins, {2} pays a share of its revenue.{6}
hist.2022.exportcontrol.title: The US restricts exports of advanced chips
hist.2022.exportcontrol.fact: On 7 October 2022 the US introduced export restrictions on advanced computing and AI chips; the thresholds were tightened on 17 October 2023. Makers answered with cut-down models such as Nvidia's A800 and H800.
hist.2022.export.rule.text: Export control on the fastest processors comes into force. Buyers turn from models above the threshold to those below it: a cut-down model helps keep sales.{6}
hist.2023.export.update.title: Export control is tightened
hist.2023.export.update.text: The threshold is lower and the share of lost buyers is higher. Check which of your processors are above the threshold now.{6}
hist.decide.export.text: {1} has processors above the export control threshold. You can comply (release a cut-down model below the threshold), ask for a licence or lobby for relief.{6}
hist.decide.export.update.text: The rules are tighter and {1} again has processors above the threshold. A licence and lobbying are available again.{6}
hist.decide.pricewar.aggressor.title: {1} is preparing a price war
hist.decide.pricewar.aggressor.text: Cutting prices in several segments will make competitors follow. Start the war or hold back? If you decline, another maker will start it.{6}
hist.decide.pricewar.follower.title: A price war in the processor market
hist.decide.pricewar.follower.text: {2} and other makers are cutting prices. You can follow, hold your prices or answer with marketing instead of discounts.{6}
hist.decide.patent.plaintiff.title: Take {2} to court?
hist.decide.patent.plaintiff.text: {2} uses solutions protected by the patents of {1}. You can sue or leave things as they are.{6}
hist.decide.patent.withdrawal.title: {2} withdraws the licence of {1}
hist.decide.patent.withdrawal.text: The technology licence is withdrawn. Arbitration is long and dear but can be won; a new licence means monthly payments; own development makes research dearer.{6}
hist.decide.patent.infringement.title: {2} accuses {1} of copying its design
hist.decide.patent.infringement.text: You can fight (there is a chance to win, but a loss costs more than a settlement), settle, or redesign.{6}
hist.1971.microprocessor.title: Intel 4004: the first microprocessor
hist.1971.microprocessor.fact: On 15 November 1971 Intel released the 4004, the first complete processor on a single chip. Industrial electronics gained an inexpensive computing part of a new class.
hist.1973.oilembargo.title: The 1973 oil crisis
hist.1973.oilembargo.fact: On 17 October 1973 Arab oil producers imposed an embargo and oil prices rose sharply. Developed economies slowed, while interest rates and inflation rose.
hist.1975.altair.title: Altair 8800 and hobby computers
hist.1975.altair.fact: In January 1975 Popular Electronics featured the Altair 8800 kit built around the Intel 8080. A mass hobbyist market for personal computers began.
hist.1977.trinity.title: Three computers of 1977
hist.1977.trinity.fact: In 1977 the ready-built personal computers Apple II, Commodore PET and TRS-80 reached the market. Buyers could for the first time get a machine without assembling it.
hist.1980.volcker.title: Volcker's high interest rates
hist.1980.volcker.fact: In 1979–1981 the US Federal Reserve raised interest rates sharply to bring down inflation. Credit became expensive, and the economy contracted in 1980–1982.
hist.1981.ibmpc.title: IBM PC and the second source
hist.1981.ibmpc.fact: On 12 August 1981 IBM released the IBM PC built around the Intel 8088. IBM required a second source for the processor, and AMD began to make it under an Intel licence.
hist.1985.dramexit.title: Intel exits the DRAM market
hist.1985.dramexit.fact: In 1985 Intel stopped making DRAM memory and concentrated on microprocessors. Japanese memory makers kept cutting prices, and competition in the entry segments intensified.
hist.1986.usjapan.title: The US–Japan semiconductor agreement
hist.1986.usjapan.fact: In 1986 the United States and Japan signed a semiconductor agreement: Japanese makers agreed not to dump chips in the US and third markets. Chip prices rose.
hist.1987.koshiba.title: The Toshiba–Kongsberg scandal
hist.1987.koshiba.fact: In 1987 Toshiba Machine supplied the Soviet Union with numerically controlled machines that violated COCOM export restrictions. The scandal brought sanctions and government criticism.
hist.1987.blackmonday.title: Black Monday
hist.1987.blackmonday.fact: On 19 October 1987 world stock markets lost more than a fifth of their value in one day. Banks tightened lending and demand for equipment temporarily fell.
hist.1987.arbitration.title: The licence withdrawal dispute
hist.1987.arbitration.fact: In 1987 Intel ended the licence under which AMD made processors, and the companies went to arbitration. The dispute lasted several years.
hist.1988.dramshortage.title: The 1988 DRAM shortage
hist.1988.dramshortage.fact: In 1988 demand for DRAM memory outpaced supply and chip prices rose. Makers of equipment faced noticeably higher costs.
hist.1991.brandprogram.title: The Intel Inside programme
hist.1991.brandprogram.fact: In 1991 Intel launched the Intel Inside programme: PC makers received advertising support if they showed the processor logo. The logo became known to buyers.
hist.1992.clonesuit.title: Intel sues Cyrix
hist.1992.clonesuit.fact: In 1992 Intel accused Cyrix of infringing rights to the 386 processor microcode. Cyrix kept selling compatible processors while the dispute ran.
hist.1994.fdiv.title: The Pentium FDIV bug
hist.1994.fdiv.fact: In November 1994 a division error in the Pentium processor became publicly known. Intel acknowledged the flaw and replaced some processors, and its costs rose.
hist.1995.win95.title: The Windows 95 launch
hist.1995.win95.fact: On 24 August 1995 Microsoft released Windows 95, and home PC sales surged. The new system made computers easier for ordinary users.
hist.1997.asiancrisis.title: The Asian financial crisis
hist.1997.asiancrisis.fact: In 1997 a currency crisis hit East Asian economies: currencies fell and exports and domestic demand dropped. Electronics firms in the region cut purchases.
hist.1998.sub1000.title: Prices below 1000 dollars
hist.1998.sub1000.fact: In 1998 Intel cut the prices of Celeron processors to make PCs cheaper than 1000 dollars. Rivals in the entry segments answered with price cuts.
hist.1999.jiji.title: The Jiji earthquake
hist.1999.jiji.fact: On 21 September 1999 an earthquake in Taiwan halted plants in the Hsinchu Science Park. Semiconductor output was disrupted.
hist.2000.dotcom.title: The dot-com crash
hist.2000.dotcom.fact: In 2000 valuations of internet companies began to collapse and technology stocks lost much of their value. Banks tightened credit and buyers cut PC purchases.
hist.2000.ghzrace.title: The gigahertz race
hist.2000.ghzrace.fact: In 2000 Intel and AMD competed on clock speed and the first 1 GHz processors reached the market. Frequency became the main buyer argument, though performance grew more slowly.
hist.2005.jftc.title: A Japanese regulator and Intel
hist.2005.jftc.fact: In 2005 the Japan Fair Trade Commission warned Intel over rebate terms for PC makers. The company changed the terms and a rival gained more room to sell.
hist.2005.archswitch.title: Apple switches to Intel
hist.2005.archswitch.fact: On 6 June 2005 Apple announced that Macs would move from PowerPC to Intel processors. Apple got a new platform and Intel got a major customer.
hist.2006.core2war.title: Core 2 and the 2006 price war
hist.2006.core2war.fact: In July 2006 Intel released the Core 2 processors, which outperformed AMD's products. The company cut prices in the high-end and mid-range segments to secure its lead.
hist.2008.netbook.title: Netbooks
hist.2008.netbook.fact: In 2008 netbooks appeared: inexpensive, small, low-power laptops that quickly became popular. Demand for low-cost processors and cheap computers grew.
hist.2008.lehman.title: The collapse of Lehman Brothers
hist.2008.lehman.fact: On 15 September 2008 Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy and the global credit crisis deepened. Demand for equipment fell and banks cut lending.
hist.2011.tohoku.title: The Tōhoku earthquake
hist.2011.tohoku.fact: On 11 March 2011 an earthquake and tsunami in north-east Japan halted electronics plants. Supplies of semiconductors and components were disrupted.
hist.2012.postpc.title: The post-PC era
hist.2012.postpc.fact: In 2012 sales of traditional PCs declined as tablets and smartphones became the main consumer purchase. Demand for desktop PCs and entry laptops fell, while the industrial segment grew.
hist.2017.corewar.title: Ryzen and the core race
hist.2017.corewar.fact: In 2017 AMD released Ryzen processors with many cores at accessible prices. Competition on core count intensified and the high-end leader cut prices.
hist.2018.meltdown.title: The Meltdown and Spectre vulnerabilities
hist.2018.meltdown.fact: In January 2018 researchers disclosed the Meltdown and Spectre vulnerabilities, which relate to speculative execution in processors. Vendors released fixes that in some cases reduced performance.
hist.2018.tradewar.title: The US–China trade war
hist.2018.tradewar.fact: In 2018 the United States imposed tariffs on Chinese goods and China responded in kind. Electronics production costs rose and supply chains had to be reorganised.
hist.2020.covid.title: The COVID-19 pandemic
hist.2020.covid.fact: In March 2020 the WHO declared the COVID-19 pandemic. The first wave reduced demand for equipment, and demand for laptops and home PCs later rose.
hist.2020.shortage.title: The global chip shortage
hist.2020.shortage.fact: A global semiconductor shortage began in late 2020 as demand outpaced fab capacity. PC and car output fell and contract prices rose.
hist.2020.insourcing.title: Apple moves to its own chips
hist.2020.insourcing.fact: In June 2020 Apple announced that it would move its Macs from Intel processors to its own Apple silicon. Third-party suppliers lost part of their contracts and OEM talks became harder.
hist.2022.chipsact.title: The CHIPS and Science Act
hist.2022.chipsact.fact: On 9 August 2022 the United States signed the CHIPS and Science Act, which provides subsidies and tax incentives for semiconductor production. The tax burden fell for manufacturers that own fabs.
hist.2023.aiboom.title: The AI boom
hist.2023.aiboom.fact: In 2023 demand for accelerators for training and running neural networks surged. High-end processors and industrial solutions gained additional demand.
hist.2017.cryptoboom.title: Crypto boom: GPU demand
hist.2017.cryptoboom.fact: In autumn 2017 a rally in cryptocurrencies led to mass purchases of graphics cards for mining and a GPU shortage. Demand stayed high until early 2018 and graphics card prices rose.
hist.2021.cryptoboom.title: The second crypto boom: graphics cards
hist.2021.cryptoboom.fact: In 2021 a new cryptocurrency rally again increased demand for mining graphics cards. GPU output could not keep up with orders and graphics card prices stayed high.

hist.news.solarfoundries.title: AMD spins off its fabs
hist.news.solarfoundries.text: {1} has spun its manufacturing off into a separate company, {2}.{6}
hist.news.solarfoundries.fact: On 2 March 2009 AMD announced that it would spin its manufacturing off into a separate company that became GlobalFoundries; an investor from Abu Dhabi took the controlling stake. AMD moved to a model without fabs of its own and kept ordering chips from the new company.
hist.news.x86license.title: The end of the x86 licence limits
hist.news.x86license.text: One of the holders of x86 licences has left the market: the limits those licences imposed no longer apply.{6}
hist.news.x86license.fact: Intel and AMD are bound by a cross-licence for the x86 architecture, which lets AMD build compatible processors. Such an agreement cannot be passed to a third company without the consent of the parties, so the exit of one of them changes the terms for every x86 maker.
